name: Muisca
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 9 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Constenla Umaña, Adolfo. 1984. Los fonemas del muisca. Estudios de Lingüística Chibcha 3: 65-111. San José: Universidad de Costa Rica. Open access:https://archivo.revistas.ucr.ac.cr/2/index.php/chibcha/article/view/24043

catalog_quote: En cuarto lugar, la posición del acento recae por lo general en la última sílaba de la palabra. En un conteo de cien palabras acentuadas no monosilábicas el resultado fue el siguiente: acentuadas en la última sílaba, 71; acentuadas en la penúltima, 13; acentuadas en la antepenúltima, 2; acentuadas tanto en la penúltima como en la última, 8; acentuadas tanto en la antepenúltima como en la última, 1; acentuadas en las tres sílabas, 5. Dieciséis de las cien palabras son apariciones de / bohotˢa / 'con', que, como se indicó en el párrafo precedente es especialmente inestable. Si se elimina dicha palabra, las 84 formas restantes se reparten en 70 acentuadas en la última sílaba (83%), 11 acentuadas en la penúltima (13%), 1 en la antepenúltima (1%) y 2 tanto en la última como en la penúltima (2%). Si se considera que el "acento" no era distintivo, se explicarían con mayor facilidad varios de los hechos mencionados ... y el predominio muy notable de la última sílaba como su receptora. Cabría pensar que en la palabra muisca se daba un aumento gradual de la prominencia (logrado por medio del incremento de la cantidad vocálica) en las tres últimas sílabas. Este aumento era mayor en la penúltima que en la antepenúltima y mayor aún en la última, en la que culminaba. No siendo distintivo, este rasgo estaría sometido a variaciones debido a factores como la emotividad y el énfasis.

new_statements.translation: Fourth, the position of the accent falls as a rule on the last syllable of the word. In a count of one hundred accented non-monosyllabic words the result was: accented on the last syllable, 71; on the penult, 13; on the antepenult, 2; on both penult and last, 8; on both antepenult and last, 1; on all three syllables, 5. [...] If one takes the 'accent' not to have been distinctive, several of the facts mentioned are more easily explained [...] and the very marked predominance of the last syllable as its bearer.

On p. 105 the quoted passage is verbatim: "En cuarto lugar, la posición del acento recae por lo general en la última sílaba de la palabra. En un conteo de cien palabras acentuadas no monosilábicas el resultado fue el siguiente: acentuadas en la última sílaba, 71; acentuadas en la penúltima, 13; acentuadas en la antepenúltima, 2; acentuadas tanto en la penúltima como en la última, 8; acentuadas tanto en la antepenúltima como en la última, 1; acentuadas en las tres sílabas, 5." and, two paragraphs down, "Si se considera…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word prominence (marked in Lugo 1619 and the Madrid confessionary by interchangeable circumflex/grave/acute signs, which Lugo says indicate a long-pronounced vowel) falls predominantly on the final syllable: excluding the unstable postposition bohotsa 'con', 70 of 84 accented polysyllables (83%) are marked final, 11 (13%) penultimate, 1 antepenultimate, 2 both. Constenla concludes the accent was probably not distinctive and hypothesises (p. 105) a gradual increase of prominence, realised as vowel lengthening, over the last three syllables, culminating on the final one; being non-distinctive, it varied with emphasis, which explains the inconsistent marking. Lugo himself (Prólogo al lector; fol. 158) only says the marked vowel is pronounced long and that he leaves the rules of accent to usage.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not treated as such. Constenla notes some words carry marks on two or three syllables (8 penult+final, 1 antepenult+final, 5 on all three of 100) and interprets this as graded prominence rising toward the final syllable rather than secondary stress. Saravia 2015 (pedagogical, p. 11) posits secondary stress on the second syllable and main stress on the last in C-V1-h-V1-C-a words (kuhubá, bohozhá).
new_statements.exceptions: Marking is very inconsistent in both sources; the same word appears accented on the final syllable at times and on the penult (exceptionally antepenult) at others; the postposition 'con' is written at least six ways (bhôhôzhâ, bhôhozhâ, bhôhozha, bhôzhâ, bhôzha, bhozhâ); the sole apparent minimal pair ayâ 'adelante' / aîa 'muy lejos' (Lugo fol. 118) is judged unreliable. Alvar 1977: 20 had instead inferred distinctive vowel quantity coinciding with the accent; Constenla argues against this. Saravia 2015: 11, 77 (course, not a description) states the opposite default (penultimate, with 1st-conjugation futures in -nga final).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('prominencia dentro de la palabra'), based on written accent marks in a 1619 printed grammar and a 17th-c. confessionary; §5.1 treats intonation separately (punctuation may reflect final/non-final intonation contours; no source describes intonation). Confidence is limited by the philological nature of the evidence.
new_statements.identity_note: Extinct language known only from colonial (1600s) missionary sources: Lugo 1619 (printed grammar), the anonymous Bogotá ms (ed. González de Pérez 1987 / Uricoechea 1871) and the Madrid ms (ed. Lucena Salmoral). Constenla's statement is a philological inference from the accent marks in Lugo 1619 and the Madrid confessionary, not from speech. Saravia 2015 (pedagogical reconstruction for the revitalisation community) posits the opposite, penultimate, rule; it is not a primary description. No dialect issue; Duit (duit1235) is a separate sister variety mentioned by Adelaar but not covered here.

tone_statements.quote: There are no indications that tone, stress, or vowel nasality were contrastive in Muisca. Although Lugo (1619) used diacritics in the context of vowels, there are too many irregularities to draw any firm conclusions in this matter. In Lugo’s work, stress is mostly (in approximately 70 to 80% of the cases) indicated on the last syllable of a word, and less frequently on the penultimate (in approximately 13% of the cases) (Constenla Umaña 1984b: 103–6).
tone_statements.locator: p. 431, sec. 2.3.18.1.1 'Muisca vowels and suprasegmentals' (end of subsection, before p. 432)
tone_statements.summary: No contrastive tone demonstrable from the colonial record; diacritics irregular; prominence mostly word-final; circumflex = non-phonemic length.

sources.note: States explicitly that there are no indications that tone (or stress, or vowel nasality) was contrastive in Muisca; Lugo's 1619 vowel diacritics are too irregular for firm conclusions, his circumflex marks (non-phonemic) vowel length, and marked prominence is mostly word-final (after Constenla 1984). At family level (p. 514) tone is attested in Bari, Boruca, Bribri, Cabecar, Chimila, Pech, Terraba, Tunebo but Proto-Chibchan tone is left unreconstructed; Muisca is cited only for (probable) final stress.

sources.citation: Constenla Umaña, Adolfo. 2008. Estado actual de la subclasificación de las lenguas chibchenses y de la reconstrucción fonológica y gramatical del protochibchense. Estudios de Lingüística Chibcha 27: 117-135. San José: Universidad de Costa Rica. Open PDF:https://archivo.revistas.ucr.ac.cr/2/index.php/chibcha/article/view/9631
sources.note: Describes another variety (Glottolog chib1249). Gives the current Proto-Chibchan phoneme inventory with a nasality prosodeme, three tonal phonemes (*1 *2 *3, revised up from the two of Constenla 1981) and an accent phoneme; tone reflexes are discussed only for Bribri/Cabecar/Boruca; nothing is said about tone in Muisca itself (Muisca appears only in segmental changes and lexicostatistics). Relevant as the family baseline against which Muisca's unrecorded tonality must be judged.
